extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors, patent litigators, and patent agents handling functional/software-related claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for drafting, prosecuting, and litigating functional (means-plus-function / 35 U.S.C. §112(f)) claim limitations, with emphasis on software/computer-implemented inventions. Covers statutory text, PTO/CAFC/PTAB tests, risks, prosecution practice, and litigation/IPR strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claiming definition
rubrics_metrics.description: “A claim term is functional when it recites a feature ‘by what it does rather than by what it is’ (e.g., as evidenced by its specific structure or specific ingredients). …There is nothing inherently wrong with defining some part of an invention in functional terms. Functional language does not, in and of itself, render a claim improper.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional language is permitted, but whether it invokes 35 U.S.C. §112(f) or renders a claim indefinite depends on context, the specification disclosure, and the knowledge of a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory standard — 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (means-plus-function)
rubrics_metrics.description: An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When §112(f) applies, claim scope is limited to the corresponding structure/material/acts disclosed in the specification and their equivalents. The slide deck also emphasizes the practical effect that §112(f) interpretation often narrows claim scope and ties claim coverage to spec disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO 3-prong test for invoking §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Per MPEP 2181(I), interpret a limitation under §112(f) if: (1) the claim limitation uses the phrase “means” or a substitute generic placeholder; (2) that phrase is modified by functional language (typically linked by “for”); and (3) the phrase is not modified by sufficient structure or material for performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply all three prongs—generic placeholder, functional modification, and lack of sufficient structure—to determine whether §112(f) should apply. The USPTO uses this test in examination and documents examples of non-means claims that should be interpreted as invoking §112(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption from use of “means for” and how to overcome it
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim uses the literal “means for” plus functional language there is a presumption that §112(f) is invoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption can be overcome if the claim term (or surrounding claim language/specification) recites sufficient structure to perform the claimed function. Examining record should document how the presumption was overcome and identify the corresponding structure in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invocation of §112(f) where “means” is not used (nonce/generic placeholders)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that does not explicitly recite “means for” may still be interpreted under §112(f) when it (1) uses a generic placeholder for structure, (2) includes functional language, and (3) lacks sufficient structure to perform the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Williamson v. Citrix weakened the strong presumption that a claim without “means” does not invoke §112(f), so courts and examiners will analyze nonce terms (e.g., “module,” “component,” “unit”) under the 3-prong test to decide. Document the analysis on the record during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient structure requirement for software/computer-implemented MPF claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For software-related means-plus-function elements, the corresponding structure required in the specification often must include the algorithm(s) that transform a general-purpose computer into a special-purpose machine (see Aristocrat; Alappat). Conversely, basic functions that any general-purpose computer can perform without special programming may not require a disclosed algorithm (see Katz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed function is specialized (requires special programming), include step‑by‑step description of the algorithm, flowcharts, or textual/pseudo-code tying the structure to the function. Cases: Aristocrat (algorithm required), EON (indefiniteness for lack of algorithm), Katz (standard microprocessor may suffice for non-specialized operations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks and benefits of a §112(f) interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking §112(f) may lead to a narrower claim interpretation limited to structures disclosed in the specification and equivalents, but it can also make invalidity attacks easier if the specification lacks corresponding structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: prior art must disclose corresponding structure/equivalents and §112(f) can help with §101 arguments in some contexts. Risks: exposure to §112(a) enablement/written-description and §112(b) indefiniteness rejections/invalidity; narrower scope can enable design-arounds and non-infringement defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining indefiniteness under §112(b) when §112(f) is implicated
rubrics_metrics.description: Two central inquiries: (1) Does the specification disclose adequate structure for performing the claimed function (e.g., algorithm for software)? (2) Is the disclosed structure linked to the claimed function, or is it mere generic hardware/black box?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If structure is missing (Aristocrat/Aristocrat-related, EON) or not linked to the function (B. Braun Medical), the limitation may be indefinite. See MPEP 2173.02 for examiner guidance. Flowcharts or algorithmic descriptions can be sufficient if they concretely tie structure to function.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO guidance on specialized vs non-specialized computer-implemented functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialized computer functions require “special programming” for a general-purpose computer; non-specialized functions are commonly performed by general-purpose computers by a POSITA (e.g., receiving, sending, storing data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-specialized functions, claim formats such as “processor configured to [function]” may avoid §112(f) (see Katz). For specialized functions, the specification should disclose algorithms and structural details. USPTO training materials and examples discuss when non-means claim language should nonetheless be treated as invoking §112(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting practices to avoid unintended invocation of §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: No bright-line language guarantees avoiding §112(f); still, practical practices include: avoid explicit use of “means” or “step” for plus a function; avoid coined/nonce terms that do not connote structure; in some cases include explicit MPF claims elsewhere in the application/continuation to vary scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider varying claim scope across independent/dependent claims and across continuations. Where the functional element is at the point of novelty, recite sub-steps or known operations to show sufficient structure and reduce §112(f) risk. There is no foolproof template—context matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification drafting practices to support functional claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft the specification to include technical descriptions, algorithms (when not off-the-shelf), flow diagrams, and explanations linking disclosed structure to claimed functions; describe how functional components interact and list alternative algorithms and examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide enough detail to support §112(a)/(b) if §112(f) is applied: specific algorithms, flowcharts, pseudo-code, interaction descriptions, and examples of alternatives/equivalents. Also consider including explicit means/step-for claims in the original filing or continuations to preserve options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention disclosure meeting checklist for functional elements
rubrics_metrics.description: For each function/component, verify whether it is off-the-shelf (OTS) or requires custom/special programming; for OTS components, obtain specific examples; for custom components, obtain algorithmic details and alternatives (flow diagrams, pseudo-code) and how components interact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drill down with inventors to capture sufficient structural detail for the specification. Collect examples of OTS implementations and document alternatives/equivalents to support later §112(f) analyses and possible MPF claim drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Clarity of the Record expectations regarding §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: When §112(f) issues are at play, examiners should document all §112(f) presumptions, explain how presumptions were overcome (if they were), identify on the record the structure in the specification that performs the function, and address specific claim limitations when relying on prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecutors should expect clearer Office Actions and should likewise record arguments and identify corresponding structure during interviews and amendments. The PTO’s pilot aimed to improve clarity around §112(f) analyses and reasons for allowance/rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation and IPR strategies concerning §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: As petitioner: argue claim indefiniteness for lack of disclosed structure and/or pursue prior-art invalidity; if a panel finds insufficient structure they may not institute on the MPF claim but state lack of corresponding structure in decision. As patent owner: argue that the broadest reasonable interpretation of an MPF claim is the disclosed structures and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine §112(f) arguments with §101 or §112(a)/(b) strategies as appropriate. For non-infringement, exploit narrower §112(f) constructions to design around. In IPRs, prepare to argue both indefiniteness and prior-art anticipation/obviousness depending on the panel’s findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents (DOE) vs MPF equivalents distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: MPF equivalents and DOE are different: timing and function tests differ. §112(f) equivalence is evaluated at issuance and requires the identical function; DOE is evaluated at the time of infringement and asks for substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After-arising technology: may not fall under §112(f) equivalence but could be covered by DOE. A finding of non-infringement under §112(f) for lack of identical function does not preclude a later DOE finding. See Ring & Pinion v. ARB for discussion of differences and interplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of Williamson v. Citrix on §112(f) presumption and claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Williamson (Fed. Cir. en banc 2015) eliminated the strong presumption that §112(f) is not invoked if a claim does not explicitly recite “means for” or “step for,” making it easier to find §112(f) invoked by nonce terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the presumption remains that claims not reciting means/step-for do not invoke §112(f), Williamson requires a more searching inquiry into whether a term is a generic placeholder lacking structural meaning to a POSITA. Practitioners should anticipate more frequent §112(f) analyses for non-means language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner focus on software-related functional limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO examination guidance emphasizes evaluating §112(f) limitations particularly in software/computer claims to provide a clear prosecution record and ensure functional claim boundaries are explained and justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners will apply training materials and examples to identify limitations that invoke §112(f) and will seek to document corresponding structures, especially for specialized computer functions requiring disclosed algorithms. Applicants should be prepared to cite spec paragraphs/figures and explain structure-function links.
